patients.label: Female infant born at 25 weeks 2 days gestation with fatal Aspergillus flavus infection

identity_evidence.quote: We report a fatal case of Aspergillus flavus infection in a 25-week infant

attribution_limitations: The authors state that the absence of fungal elements in the mother's placenta and the lack of disease in the twin strongly suggest a postnatal, healthcare-associated source. This is author inference, not a documented source of infection.
Antibiotics discontinued on D2 are not named; the infant also received empiric ampicillin and gentamicin for 36 hours after birth, and broad spectrum antibiotics were started after transfer.
Species identification by MALDI-TOF was "subsequently confirmed" after the D6 culture growth and prompted the switch to voriconazole; neither the confirmation nor the switch is dated.

Silver sulfadiazine "was considered" in the discussion alongside general statements about contraindications in preterm infants; whether it was ordered or withheld for this patient is not stated, and the topical amphotericin B statement is the authors' decision that its use was not feasible or appropriate.
The authors state the right ACA and MCA infarcts may still represent vascular complications of angioinvasive Aspergillus infection even though autopsy found no fungal elements in the brain.
The authors call the amphotericin B MIC of 4 μg/mL polyene resistance in their isolate and cite wild-type ranges from the literature; no breakpoint exists for the organism.

evidence.quote: Rapidly progressive violaceous and necrotic lesions on the infant's back with central darkening concerning for invasive fungal infection.
a) A. flavus produces hyaline septate hyphae with vesicles that support phialides with spore production
b) A. flavus grows well on routine fungal media producing a powdery yellow-green colony within 7 days at 30 °C

claims.text: On day of life six a small right flank ecchymosis progressed over 6–12 hours to the entire back. She was emergently transferred to a level IV NICU for concern for possible invasive infection. A pre-transfer wound culture showed no organisms on Gram stain and no fungal growth. Labs showed WBC 21.1, platelets 146 and CRP 4.5. Broad spectrum antibiotics and liposomal amphotericin B were started after transfer, frozen section biopsy showed fungal elements concerning for Rhizopus and Aspergillus, and surgical debridement of the back was performed within 6 hours of transfer with four additional debridements on D1 and D2; antibiotics were stopped on D2.
